lead: A test team generates numbers all day: cases run, cases passed, defects raised, hours spent. A metric is one of those numbers, defined precisely so that it answers a question and helps someone decide — ship or wait, hire or automate, tighten exit criteria or relax them. Metrics appear in the daily test report, in the release go/no-go meeting, and in the retrospective that asks why defects escaped. The idea is simple: measure what you will act on, watch the trend rather than one reading, and never turn a measure into a target.
prereq: You need: 5.1 for exit criteria, which most of these metrics feed, and 5.2 for the report the numbers go into.

blocks.text: A base measure is a count taken directly from the work: test cases executed, defects logged, hours spent, failures observed. A derived metric is computed from two or more base measures, such as defects per thousand lines of code. Base measures are cheap and honest. Derived metrics carry an interpretation, so always state the formula beside the number.

items: Product metric: describes the software — defect density, coverage, availability.
Process metric: describes how the team works — test cycle time, automation coverage, defect removal efficiency.
Leading indicator: moves before the outcome, such as the open defect backlog in week 3. It lets you steer.
Lagging indicator: reports after the outcome, such as field failures in the first six months. It tells you whether steering worked.

blocks.text: Goal–Question–Metric (GQM) keeps a metric tied to a purpose. Start from a goal, write the questions that would show whether it is met, then pick the metric that answers each question.

items: State the goal as purpose, object and focus: reduce escaped defects in the payments module before release.
Write the questions: how many defects escaped last time, and at which stage?
Name a metric and its raw data for each question: defect leakage, from defects found before and after release.
Collect it, report it, and drop the metric if nobody changed a decision because of it.

blocks.text: Execution progress answers the simplest question in test management: are we running the plan? A case counts as executed once it has a result — pass, fail or blocked. A blocked case cannot run because a build, environment or test data is missing; it is not a pass.

blocks.where: executed is the number of baseline test cases with any result; planned is the number in the approved baseline. Pass rate = (passed ÷ executed) × 100, and passed + failed + blocked = executed.

blocks.text: Coverage measures how much of the product the tests actually touched. Requirement coverage is the share of requirements with at least one passing test. Statement coverage is the share of executable statements the suite ran. Branch coverage is the share of decision outcomes taken; a decision has two outcomes, so it demands more than statement coverage on the same code.
Statement coverage (%) = (statements executed ÷ executable statements) × 100; Branch coverage (%) = (branches taken ÷ total branches) × 100
blocks.where: a branch is one outcome of a decision, the true side and the false side counted separately; a statement is one executable line. Requirement coverage has the same shape: requirements with a passing test ÷ total requirements × 100.

items: Automation coverage = automated cases ÷ total cases × 100 (see 5.3).
Test cycle time = hours from build ready to the test result signed off. Falling cycle time is what makes daily builds possible.

blocks.text: Defect density normalises a defect count by size so two releases can be compared. Size may be KLOC, requirements or test cases — say which, and give the unit.

blocks.where: defects is the count found in a stated phase, say system testing; size is thousands of lines of code (KLOC), number of requirements, or number of test cases. Write 6 defects/KLOC, not 6.

blocks.text: Defect removal efficiency, DRE (%) = (D_pre ÷ (D_pre + D_post)) × 100; Defect leakage (%) = (D_post ÷ (D_pre + D_post)) × 100
blocks.where: D_pre is defects found before delivery across all test phases; D_post is defects found after delivery, usually in the first months of use. The two percentages add to 100%.

blocks.text: Severity distribution is a short table — critical, high, medium, low — not a single index; two projects with 100 defects each can be very different. For the trend, plot cumulative defect arrival against cumulative closure; the vertical gap between the curves is the open backlog.
MTBF = total operating time ÷ number of failures; Availability (%) = (MTBF ÷ (MTBF + MTTR)) × 100
blocks.where: MTBF is mean time between failures in hours; MTTR is mean time to repair in hours; availability is the share of time the system is up.

sections.h3: Trends, variance and the danger of targets

blocks.text: One reading says little. Plot each metric against time and read the slope: a pass rate falling late in a cycle usually means risky late changes, not a suddenly poor team. Compare a release with its own past, not with another product.
Effort variance (%) = ((actual effort − planned effort) ÷ planned effort) × 100
blocks.where: schedule variance uses the same shape with days. Positive means overrun and negative means under; state the sign convention or the reader will guess wrong.

blocks.text: Two pitfalls break more metric programmes than anything else. First, when a metric becomes a target people optimise the number instead of the goal: demand 2 defects/KLOC and teams stop logging trivial defects, or split one defect into five. Second, comparing across dissimilar projects — a 15 KLOC web tool against a 500 KLOC embedded system — ignores domain, age and process. Compare trends within a project.

figure.caption: The worked example's own counts: 90 defects found in test plus 10 found after release give DRE 90% and leakage 10% — the number to raise at the go/no-go meeting — while 1140 of 1200 planned cases executed give 95% progress.

spec.title: Worked example: 15 KLOC release
spec.aria: The worked example's base counts flow into derived metrics: 90 defects in test plus 10 after release make a total of 100, giving DRE 90% and leakage 10%, while 1140 executed of 1200 planned cases give execution progress of 95%.

examples.question: A release is 15 KLOC. Testing found 90 defects; the first six months after release found 10 more. Across installations the system ran 5000 hours with 8 failures. Of 1200 planned test cases, 1140 were executed (900 passed, 180 failed, 60 blocked). Compute defect density, defect removal efficiency, defect leakage, MTBF and test execution progress. Which number would you raise at the go/no-go meeting?
steps: Read together: density is unremarkable, but leakage of 10% says the exit criteria let too many defects through.
examples.answer: Density 6 defects/KLOC, DRE 90%, leakage 10%, MTBF 625 hours, execution progress 95%; leakage is the number to raise, because it shows the exit criteria were too loose.
examples.check:
kloc = 15
test_defects = 90
post_defects = 10
hours = 5000
failures = 8
executed = 1140
planned = 1200
density = test_defects / kloc
dre = test_defects / (test_defects + post_defects) * 100
leak = post_defects / (test_defects + post_defects) * 100
mtbf = hours / failures
progress = executed / planned * 100
print(density)
print(dre)
print(leak)
print(mtbf)
print(progress)

examples.question: A system runs 2000 hours with 4 failures; mean time to repair is 5 hours. Compute MTBF and availability.
steps: The repair time barely moves availability here; at MTTR = 50 hours it would fall to 90.9%.
examples.answer: MTBF is 500 hours and availability is 99.0%.
examples.check:
hours = 2000
failures = 4
mttr = 5
mtbf = hours / failures
avail = mtbf / (mtbf + mttr) * 100
print(mtbf)
print(round(avail, 2))

traps: Quoting a metric without formula or unit: '6 defects' instead of '6 defects per KLOC' loses marks and misleads the reader.
Mixing DRE and leakage denominators. Both divide by (D_pre + D_post), not by D_pre alone, and they add to 100%.
Assuming a high defect count means a weak team. A team that logs many defects early usually delivers a cleaner release; a low count can mean poor reporting.
Turning a measure into a target: demand a density figure and the data improves, not the software.
Comparing coverage figures across projects; 80% branch coverage of a small script is not the same achievement as 80% of a payments engine.

quiz.q: Define base measure and derived metric, with one example of each.
quiz.a: A base measure is a count taken directly, such as test cases executed or defects logged. A derived metric is computed from base measures, such as defect density = defects ÷ KLOC.

quiz.q: Write the formula for MTBF and give its unit.
quiz.a: MTBF = total operating time ÷ number of failures, in hours.

quiz.q: Why is the open defect backlog a leading indicator while defect leakage is a lagging one?
quiz.a: The backlog is visible during testing and predicts whether the release will be clean, so you can still act. Leakage needs post-release data, so it only reports how good the earlier decision was.

quiz.q: A product is 20 KLOC. Testing finds 80 defects and 20 more appear in the first year of use. Compute defect density, DRE and leakage.
Of 800 planned test cases, 600 executed: 400 passed, 150 failed, 50 blocked. Compute execution progress and pass rate.
Requirement coverage is 96%, yet the pass rate fell sharply in the final week. Give two plausible explanations and the data that separates them.
quiz.a: Either late changes broke working features, or testers are now running harder, previously blocked cases. Separate them with the defect arrival trend and a list of builds changed in that week: a late spike in critical defects points to risky changes, not to better testing.

quiz.q: A manager announces 'zero defects may escape' as a target. Leakage falls but field failures rise. Explain.
quiz.a: The metric became a target, so defects are under-reported or reclassified before release. The number improved while the software did not. Fix it by tracking field failures directly and treating leakage as a trend, not a quota.

beyond: Not for the exam. Release dashboards in industry mix these numbers with delivery metrics such as lead time for change and change failure rate. Reliability growth models fit a curve to failure times to predict when a failure-rate target will be met. Defect prediction models rank files by likely fault density so test effort goes where it pays. Search for 'goal question metric', 'defect leakage benchmark' and 'reliability growth model' to go further.
